wv_upper_meadow.blurb: A string of sport buttresses along the north bank of the Meadow River, in the most remote part of the New River Gorge region. Zero, First, Second, Third and Fourth Buttress, plus Cambodia and Shaved Box Canyon, make up the climbing. It is almost entirely sport, with a little trad, and it is hard: most routes fall between 5.10 and 5.12, with only a few below 5.9 and a few at 5.13. The gorge is known for bullet-hard sandstone. Most crags catch afternoon sun, and First Buttress stays dry in the rain. The walk from river level to the walls follows an old jeep trail and takes about 5 to 20 minutes.

bc_east_kootenay_2.blurb: A climbing region in southeastern British Columbia, set between the Rocky Mountains on the east and the Purcells on the west, with Cranbrook as its main town. Nearly everything here is sport, with a little trad, and the grades are on the hard side: a core of 5.10 to 5.12, some 5.13 and only a thin set of moderates. Lakit Lake is the largest cluster, a small crag known for steep, pumpy climbing on white quartzite that often stays dry. Lumberton and Buffalo Tail add more sport, and smaller walls like Tora Bora Crag and Secret Spires fill out the region. Rock quality is generally better in the Purcells.

bc_southern_crags.blurb: A cluster of crags in Skaha Bluffs, on a hillside above Skaha Lake just south of Penticton. Sport routes lead, with a fair amount of trad and a few top-rope lines. The Southern Crags are very popular, partly because of the short walk in, and they hold many easy and moderate climbs alongside plenty at 5.10 to 5.12. The harder 5.11s and 5.12s are concentrated at The Wave, while Diamondback, Raven's Castle and Elusive Edge fill out the rest. Skaha as a whole is coarse-grained gneiss, with cliffs generally under 30 metres tall, set in parallel canyons, and the weather there is mild.

ca_truckee_river_canyon.blurb: The canyon runs from the outlet of Lake Tahoe down to the California border, with the crags perched above Highway 89. The cliffs are basalt, and the climbing mixes plenty of sport with a fairly large selection of traditional routes. Most routes sit in the 5.9 to 5.12 range, centered on 5.10 and 5.11. Big Chief is the largest group of routes, a steep, bolted wall over 250 feet high, while Twin Crags is formed of basalt columns and stays climbable in winter when many other crags are snowed in. Deep Creek Crags and Shirley Canyon Cliffs are smaller. Approaches are usually snow-free from about April or May through late December, and in a dry year the canyon may be climbable year-round.

ut_cedar_canyon_2.blurb: A canyon east of Cedar City in southwest Utah, climbed along Highway 14 on many separate walls rather than one big crag. Sport routes lead, with a good amount of bouldering, some trad and a little aid. Roped grades mostly run from 5.9 to 5.12, with a thin set of easier lines. The terrain ranges from steep slab through vertical to overhanging, with some good rock mixed with a lot of loose stone. Spring and fall are the best seasons, though summer climbing is possible, and the canyon also holds ice in winter. Graveside Matter Wall is the largest cluster, followed by Bowling Alley and the Cedar Slide boulders.
